Ring a bell
ring a bel
Sound vaguely familiar — Sonarle a uno.
That name rings a bell.
Usually about a name or fact you half remember.
Sit on the fence
sit on da fens
Refuse to take a side — Nadar entre dos aguas / no mojarse.
Stop sitting on the fence and decide.
Also: a fence-sitter.
Take with a grain of salt
téik uith a gréin ov solt
Not believe something completely — Tomar con pinzas / con reservas.
Take his advice with a grain of salt.
British English: with a pinch of salt.
Under your nose
ánder yor nóus
Right in front of you, though you did not notice — En tus narices / delante de las narices.
The keys were under my nose the whole time.
Also: right under someone's nose.
A storm in a teacup
a storm in a tíikap
A lot of fuss about something unimportant — Una tormenta en un vaso de agua.
The argument was a storm in a teacup.
American English: a tempest in a teapot.
Burn the midnight oil
bern da mídnait óil
Work or study very late — Quemarse las pestañas / trasnochar estudiando.
She burned the midnight oil before the exam.
Forms: burns, burned, burned the midnight oil.
Hit the books
jit da buks
Start studying hard — Ponerse a estudiar / hincar los codos.
I need to hit the books this weekend.
Informal. Forms: hits, hit, hit the books.
In hot water
in jot uóter
In trouble — En apuros / con el agua al cuello.
He's in hot water with his boss.
Also: get into hot water.
Keep your chin up
kiip yor chin ap
Stay cheerful in a hard time — No desanimarse / mantener el ánimo.
Keep your chin up, things will improve.
Usually said as encouragement.
On the back burner
on da bak bérner
Left for later, with low priority — En segundo plano / aparcado.
The project is on the back burner for now.
Also: put something on the back burner.
Take a rain check
téik a réin chek
Refuse now but accept another time — Dejarlo para otro día.
I'll take a rain check on dinner tonight.
A polite way to say no. American in origin.
A breeze
a bríiz
Something very easy — Coser y cantar / una tontería.
The test was a breeze.
Also: breeze through something.
Come rain or shine
kam réin or sháin
Whatever happens — Pase lo que pase / llueva o truene.
He runs every morning, come rain or shine.
Goes at the end of the sentence.
Jump on the bandwagon
yamp on da bánduagon
Join something because it has become popular — Subirse al carro / apuntarse a la moda.
Everyone jumped on the bandwagon after the win.
Slightly critical.
The best of both worlds
da best ov bóuth uérlds
The advantages of two different things at once — Lo mejor de los dos mundos.
Working from home two days gives me the best of both worlds.
Used with have or get.
Add insult to injury
ad ínsalt tu ínyuri
Make a bad situation worse — Para colmo / echar sal en la herida.
To add insult to injury, they charged me for the repair.
Usually as a linking phrase at the start.
Barking up the wrong tree
bárking ap da rong trii
Pursuing the wrong idea or person — Equivocarse de medio a medio / ir desencaminado.
If you think I took it, you're barking up the wrong tree.
Used with be.
By the skin of your teeth
bai da skin ov yor tiith
Only just; barely — Por los pelos.
We caught the train by the skin of our teeth.
Goes at the end of the sentence.
Every cloud has a silver lining
évri kláud jas a sílver láining
Every bad situation has something good in it — No hay mal que por bien no venga.
You lost that job, but every cloud has a silver lining.
A proverb; often shortened to a silver lining.
Get your act together
guet yor akt tuguéder
Start organising yourself properly — Ponerse las pilas / espabilar.
You need to get your act together before Monday.
Informal but not rude.
Go the extra mile
góu di ékstra máil
Do more than is required — Hacer un esfuerzo extra / ir más allá.
She always goes the extra mile for customers.
Positive. Forms: goes, went, gone the extra mile.
Hang in there
jang in déer
Keep going through a hard time — Aguantar / no rendirse.
Hang in there, the worst is over.
Said as encouragement.
In the same boat
in da séim bóut
In the same difficult situation — En el mismo barco.
We're all in the same boat with these prices.
Used with be.
It takes two to tango
it téiks tuu tu tángou
Both people are responsible — Dos no se pelean si uno no quiere.
Don't blame only her — it takes two to tango.
A proverb; used whole.
To make a long story short
tu méik a long stóri short
To get to the point quickly — En resumen / para abreviar.
To make a long story short, we missed the flight.
British English: to cut a long story short.
No pain no gain
nóu péin nóu guéin
You must suffer a little to achieve something — Sin esfuerzo no hay recompensa / quien algo quiere, algo le cuesta.
My legs ache, but no pain no gain.
A proverb; used whole.
Off the top of my head
of da top ov mai jed
Without checking or thinking carefully — Así de memoria / a bote pronto.
Off the top of my head, about thirty people came.
Signals that the figure may not be exact.
Pull yourself together
pul yorsélf tuguéder
Regain control of your emotions — Serenarse / recomponerse.
Pull yourself together, we have work to do.
Can sound harsh; say it gently.
Rub someone the wrong way
rab sámuan da rong uéi
Irritate someone without quite knowing why — Caer mal / sacar de quicio.
His manner rubs me the wrong way.
British English: rub someone up the wrong way.
Steal someone's thunder
stiil sámuans thánder
Take the attention that should have gone to someone else — Robar el protagonismo a.
She announced it first and stole his thunder.
Forms: steals, stole, stolen someone's thunder.
The tip of the iceberg
da tip ov di áisberg
Only a small visible part of a much bigger problem — La punta del iceberg.
These complaints are just the tip of the iceberg.
Used with be.
Through thick and thin
thruu thik and thin
In good times and bad — En las buenas y en las malas.
They stayed together through thick and thin.
Goes at the end of the sentence.
Under the table
ánder da téibl
Secretly and usually illegally — Bajo cuerda / en negro.
He was paid under the table.
Usually about money or work.
Wrap your head around
rap yor jed aráund
Manage to understand something difficult — Hacerse a la idea de / llegar a entender.
I can't wrap my head around these rules.
Informal. Often in the negative.
You can say that again
yu kan séi dat aguén
I completely agree — Y que lo digas / ya lo creo.
"It's freezing." "You can say that again."
A fixed reply; never changed.
A dime a dozen
a dáim a dázen
Very common and of little value — Del montón / los hay a patadas.
Cheap phone cases are a dime a dozen.
American English; a dime is ten cents.
Back to square one
bak tu skuéer uán
Back to the beginning after failing — Vuelta a empezar / a la casilla de salida.
The deal collapsed, so we're back to square one.
Used with be or go.
Bend over backwards
bend óuver bákuards
Try extremely hard to help someone — Desvivirse por / hacer lo imposible.
They bent over backwards to fix my booking.
Forms: bends, bent, bent over backwards.
Break a leg
bréik a leg
Good luck, said to a performer — ¡Mucha mierda! / ¡suerte!
Break a leg tonight!
Said before a performance; never literal.
Call the shots
kol da shots
Be the one who decides — Cortar el bacalao / mandar.
In this office she calls the shots.
Forms: calls, called, called the shots.
Cut corners
kat kórners
Do something badly to save time or money — Hacer chapuzas / escatimar.
They cut corners and the roof leaked.
Always critical.
Down to earth
dáun tu erth
Practical and unpretentious — Con los pies en la tierra / sencillo/a.
For a famous actor he is very down to earth.
Used with be. A compliment.
Draw the line
dro da láin
Set a limit on what you will accept — Poner límites / trazar la raya.
I don't mind helping, but I draw the line at lying.
Pattern: draw the line at something.
